titulo.texto: The Orthopedic Leg and the Red Boot

frase_gancho.texto: “Feet, what do I need them for if I have wings to fly?”: Frida added little bells and dragons to her prosthesis.

puente_narrativo.texto: Move on to the clothing display cases, where the Tehuana dresses are.

guion_corto.texto: In nineteen fifty-three, Frida had her right leg amputated below the knee because of gangrene. In her diary she wrote a line that became famous: feet, what do I need them for if I have wings to fly. Later she had an orthopedic leg made of leather, and she did not want a sad shoe. She turned it into a red boot, with little bells and Chinese dragon motifs. It is a medical object, but also an object of pride. Every step made the little bells ring. Look at the red, the details, and the shape. A prosthesis can say a lot about the person who wears it. Come closer to the display case and notice the red.

guion_largo.texto:
This is one of the most moving pieces in the hall. An orthopedic leg made of leather with a red boot. It was made between nineteen fifty-three and nineteen fifty-four, in Mexico. But it is not an ordinary prosthesis, because Frida personalized it.

To understand the boot, we need to remember what happened. Since childhood, Frida's right leg had been thinner and shorter because of polio. The accident of nineteen twenty-five fractured it in eleven places. Over the years, her circulation problems worsened and gangrene appeared. In August of nineteen fifty-three, her right leg was amputated below the knee.

It was a harsh blow. Frida wrote in her diary a line that became famous: feet, what do I need them for if I have wings to fly. It is a beautiful line, and also a difficult one. We do not know how much of it was courage and how much was a way of protecting herself. Surely a little of both.

When she was given the orthopedic leg, Frida made it her own. The boot is made of red leather. The Victoria and Albert Museum describes it as a red platform boot with small bells and Chinese dragon motifs. It is an unexpected detail, because no one would expect such luxury on a medical device. But that was who she was. She did not want to hide what was happening to her. She wanted it to be seen in its own colors.

This connects with her way of living. Throughout her life, Frida transformed what limited her into part of her image. She painted her corsets. She showed her wounds in her paintings. And she also adorned her prosthesis. It was not a naive attitude. It was a way of taking control over how others saw her.

Frida kept a diary in which she mixed texts and drawings. In it she wrote down ideas, memories, poems, and thoughts. The line about feet and wings comes from that notebook, and it helps us understand how she spoke about her body. With humor, with rawness, and also with poetry.

It has been said that she wrote the line next to a drawing of a pair of feet, in her diary. If you look at the boot in the display case with that line in mind, the object takes on a different meaning. It is no longer just a prosthesis, but the answer of a person who decided to have wings even though she was missing a foot.

Stay a moment in front of the display case. Notice the red of the leather, the shape of the boot, and the care in the details. Behind this piece is a person who decided that, even here, there was room for color.

texto.Date of the amputation: August 1953, of the right leg below the knee
texto.Object: orthopedic leather leg with red boot, 1953 to 1954, Mexico
texto.Details: red platform, small bells, and Chinese dragon motifs, according to the Victoria and Albert Museum

texto.pregunta: Myth: Frida's red boot was just an ornament, unrelated to her health.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was part of an orthopedic leather leg that she used after the amputation of nineteen fifty-three. Frida decorated it with little bells and dragons to make it her own.
